To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in nonintegrable systems that are constrained by two conservation laws the long time behavior of the system is determined by the entropy production rate, which is a measure of the degree of nonintegrability of the system.
the long time behavior in constrained, modulation unstable systems is universal and can be explained by simple arguments involving entropy and the conservation laws.

1) In nonintegrable systems, the entropy production rate per degree of freedom, $s$, is bounded from below by the Lyapunov exponent $\lambda$. 2) In nonintegrability-constrained, modulational instability systems, $\lambda$ is bounded from below and above by the rate at which the conserved quantities are being pumped in, and by the inverse of the characteristic time scale for the decay of the large scale coherent structures, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the long time behavior of nonlinear systems.
the study of coherent structures and the associated entropy in constrained nonintegrable systems, with particular emphasis on systems with modulationally unstable dynamics.
the long-time dynamics of nonintegrable, modulationally unstable systems with more than one conservation laws.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the universal behavior is a consequence of the thermodynamics of the systems, which is in turn determined by the conservation laws of the systems, and that this thermodynamics can be understood in terms of the underlying Hamiltonian structure of the system.
the entropy of the system increases with time, and that the increase is proportional to the logarithm of time.

the universal behavior observed in the long-time evolution of the constrained systems is a direct consequence of the fact that the system is a non-integrable system with a modulational instability and is not a consequence of the presence of the constraints.

we have shown that a large class of nonintegrable systems, when constrained by conservation laws, exhibit a universal behavior which can be described in terms of the entropy of the system.
the entropy of the constrained, nonintegrable system grows linearly in time and is proportional to the number of degrees of freedom.
we show that the entropy production rate is a measure of the degree of coherence.

the long time behavior of these systems can be explained by a simple, intuitive, thermodynamic model.
in such systems, the entropy of the fluctuations is the key quantity that determines the long time behavior.
